text: The pure-play public OPM universe is thin after industry consolidation and stress; private firms such as Risepoint may be better operating benchmarks than investable candidates.
LOPE should remain the primary public-company candidate for outsourced university operating-stack exposure due to explicit services agreements and revenue-share economics with university partners.
COUR should be tracked as an OPM-adjacent platform candidate, especially if degree programs and university partnerships become more material relative to consumer course revenue.
APEI is a speculative shadow candidate, useful for demand read-through into online workforce degree programs but not a direct vendor for the outsourcing node.
Key survival tests for this node are partner enrollment growth, student acquisition cost, retention/completion outcomes, revenue-share regulatory risk, and university partner concentration.
LOPE is the cleanest US-listed direct supplier candidate for online program enablement and university outsourcing because revenue is explicitly tied to services agreements with university partners.
COUR should be tracked as a platform/distribution model for university online degrees and credentials, not as a traditional full-service OPM.
STRA offers a second-order path into online degree demand through employer education-benefit administration and transferable online general-education credits.

Many historically important OPM assets are private, sold, merged, or delisted; later layers should map private reference competitors such as Risepoint/Academic Partnerships and former OPM assets at Pearson/Wiley to benchmark public candidates.
LOPE is the cleanest US-listed direct proxy for outsourced university operating-stack exposure, but later layers must stress-test GCU concentration, regulatory pressure, and partner diversification.
GHC/Kaplan is a hidden OPM/service-provider mapping inside a diversified holding company; the Purdue Global TOSA may be a long-duration customer dependency worth isolating.
COUR is a small-cap platform/distribution proxy for online degrees; degree revenue mix and learner-to-degree conversion are the key evidence gates.

Private OPM leaders such as Risepoint/Academic Partnerships and Boundless Learning appear central to the node but are not US-listed; use them as private-market benchmarks for public candidate comparison rather than as tradable candidates.

The likely chokepoint is not generic LMS software alone but the integrated bundle of compliant student acquisition, enrollment conversion, retention support, course operations, analytics, and university-specific contract execution.
LOPE should remain the primary US-listed reference candidate for the online program enablement node because its filings directly disclose a full-stack university services model.
COUR should be tracked as an underfollowed platform-style exposure to university online degrees and credentials, but degree economics require more verification after the 2025 reporting change.
LRN is an adjacent virtual education operations candidate rather than a higher-ed OPM; include only in second-order screens focused on reusable online learning infrastructure and career pathways.

Many important OPM names are not currently clean US-listed equities: Academic Partnerships/Risepoint is private, Pearson sold its OPM business to Regent, and 2U went through Chapter 11, limiting public-market purity.

Key survival tests for this node are partner enrollment growth, marketing efficiency, student retention, regulatory pressure on revenue-share and third-party-servicer models, and customer concentration.
Pearson plc is the reference public leader for high-stakes certification/licensure exam delivery and online proctoring via Pearson VUE/OnVUE.
Duolingo is a mid-cap public assessment-integrity candidate because DET is a high-stakes remote admissions test hidden inside a broader consumer edtech story.
Mitek Systems is a small-cap second-order identity-proofing hypothesis for exam security; must verify actual education, proctoring, certification, or university customers.

HealthStream is a small-cap regulated workforce credentialing/compliance platform with adjacent assessment-integrity exposure in healthcare; verify whether it touches proctored exam delivery or only credential records.

Many pure-play proctoring leaders appear private or nonprofit-owned, including Meazure Learning/ProctorU/Examity, Prometric/ETS, Kryterion, and Caveon; this limits direct public-market purity and increases the importance of second-order supplier mapping.

Pure-play assessment-integrity vendors are mostly private/nonprofit-owned, reducing the number of clean US-listed small/mid-cap candidates. Public discovery should therefore search second-order identity, fraud, secure-browser, test-delivery, and compliance-documentation suppliers.
Pearson plc / PSO should remain the reference benchmark for professional certification and remote proctoring via Pearson VUE OnVUE, but it is not an underfollowed small/mid-cap candidate.
Duolingo / DUOL is a reference example of vertically integrated online testing security through Duolingo English Test, with direct but not supplier-style node exposure.

Mitek Systems / MITK is the strongest underfollowed public hypothesis in this pass because its digital identity-verification software maps to remote exam identity proofing, but direct education/proctoring revenue evidence is still required.

Intellicheck / IDN is a speculative shadow candidate below the preferred market-cap threshold; retain only if subsequent evidence shows education, licensing-board, proctoring-platform, or credentialing integrations.

The chokepoint appears less like physical equipment scarcity and more like a regulated trust stack: identity proofing, secure exam driver/browser, live or asynchronous proctoring operations, AI flagging, human review, web monitoring, data forensics, privacy compliance, and appeal/audit documentation.

Pure-play remote proctoring and secure-browser vendors appear mostly private or nonprofit-owned; public-market exposure is more likely through Pearson, Duolingo, identity-verification vendors, background/credential verification platforms, or diversified education/testing companies.

MITK is a small-cap underfollowed hypothesis for the identity-proofing/fraud-detection layer of online exam security; survival requires proof of education, proctoring, credentialing, or public-sector exam customers.

FA is an adjacent underfollowed workforce-credential verification candidate rather than a direct exam-security vendor; survival requires evidence that online education/certification volume drives education, license, or credential verification demand.

The node's chokepoint feature bundle appears to include secure test application/browser, government-ID capture, biometric/face matching, room/environment scan, AI fraud detection, human proctor review, audit/compliance documentation, accessibility, and appeal/review workflows.
PSO/Pearson should remain the reference anchor for the assessment-integrity node because Pearson VUE/OnVUE is a direct professional-certification and online-proctoring asset.
DUOL deserves a separate DET-focused line of research: the market may price Duolingo as consumer edtech while the English Test is a high-stakes remote-assessment and proctoring asset.
MITK is an underfollowed second-order identity/fraud supplier hypothesis; keep only if future evidence shows education, exam-security, proctoring, or credentialing customers.
BKYI is a micro-cap speculative shadow candidate with education IAM evidence, but exam-security exposure and financial durability require strict falsification checks.

Many pure-play proctoring/testing vendors in this node appear private or PE-owned, including Meazure Learning/ProctorU, Proctorio, Prometric, PSI, and Kryterion; public-market mapping may therefore require looking at parents, suppliers, identity vendors, or customers.
HSTM should be carried forward as the cleanest underfollowed direct pure-play candidate for healthcare continuing education, compliance learning, credentialing, and workforce training.
GHC should be carried forward as a hidden-asset candidate because Kaplan’s professional licensure/certification/continuing-education exposure is embedded inside a diversified holding company.

APEI should be tracked as a regulated nursing credential pathway asset rather than a pure content vendor; survival in later layers depends on NCLEX pass rates, accreditation, enrollment growth, clinical placement capacity, and segment margin evidence.
ATGE is a reference leader for healthcare education and licensure-linked degree pathways; useful as a benchmark for demand strength, but less underfollowed than HSTM/GHC/APEI.

Need separate follow-up searches for legal/accounting CE, public-safety training, skilled-trades credential content, and cybersecurity certification vendors; many best-fit assets may be private, acquired, or hidden in diversified information-services companies.

For this node, the strongest bottleneck variables to verify are proprietary/approved content, accreditation or state-board alignment, exam pass-rate reputation, clinical or employer distribution channels, renewal-cycle recurrence, and evidence that content is not easily substitutable.

HealthStream is the cleanest underfollowed US-listed candidate for the workforce credential content node because it combines healthcare learning, competency, credentialing, privileging, enrollment, scheduling, and compliance workflows in a small-cap public company.

Graham Holdings/Kaplan is a hidden-content candidate: professional licensure, certification, corporate training, and continuing education are material enough to investigate, but the exposure is embedded in a diversified holding company.
Pearson should be retained as a reference anchor for scaled professional assessment/testing infrastructure rather than as the primary underfollowed discovery idea.

Skillsoft is a speculative shadow candidate: it has enterprise compliance and certification-training relevance, but micro-cap size, revenue pressure, and turnaround risk mean it should not advance without stronger evidence of recurring regulated-content demand.

The node appears strongest where credential content is paired with regulated workflow infrastructure: healthcare licensure/credentialing, professional assessment/testing, and employer-mandated compliance training.

Need a later pass to search private-to-public dependencies: Relias, UWorld, Ascend Learning, CE Broker, BoardVitals, nursing board CE registries, professional associations, and testing-center vendors may reveal public parents, suppliers, or acquirers not captured in this US-listed screen.
HSTM should be tracked as the highest-purity underfollowed candidate for healthcare continuing education, credentialing, compliance, competency, and license-monitoring infrastructure.
LRN's MedCerts exposure creates a credential-training angle hidden inside a broader K-12 and career-learning company; later layers should separate Career Learning economics from General Education.
ATGE is a reference healthcare-education operator, not the underfollowed alpha lane, but it anchors demand for regulated healthcare professional pathways.

Need a separate search pass for niche legal/accounting CPE, cybersecurity certification prep, public-safety training, and skilled-trades certification assets; this pass skewed healthcare-heavy because available public evidence was strongest there.

The best chokepoint indicators for this node are not raw learner counts alone, but accreditation alignment, exam-pass reputation, employer/channel partnerships, renewal-cycle recurrence, regulatory compliance integration, and switching cost inside enterprise workflows.
HSTM should be prioritized in later layers as the cleanest small-cap direct mapping to healthcare continuing education, licensure tracking, workforce learning, and credentialing software.
PRDO is a hypothesis-level hidden-asset candidate because Hippo Education may provide CME and exam-prep exposure, but materiality is unverified.
GHC offers a diversified-holdco route to Kaplan professional education and test prep; it may be under-screened because Kaplan is only one segment inside Graham Holdings.

For regulated professions, the chokepoint may be less about general online learning platforms and more about accredited content, CE-credit tracking, professional exam-prep reputation, and employer or association distribution.

Need a later pass across legal/accounting CE, public-safety training, skilled-trades licensing, and cybersecurity certification because many leaders are private or embedded in information-services companies.
ATGE should remain a reference/direct-capacity anchor for healthcare education because clinical affiliation agreements are explicitly disclosed as a growth constraint.
LOPE is a strong underfollowed candidate for the clinical/lab capacity node via Orbis and off-campus ABSN laboratory sites; verify ABSN site economics and clinical-network dependence.
UTI is a direct physical-capacity candidate across trades and Concorde healthcare programs; track campus opening cadence, student starts, placement rates, and employer/manufacturer partnerships.

HSTM is not proven as a clinical-placement platform, but it is a speculative-shadow software/data candidate tied to credentialing, clinical development, compliance, scheduling, and nursing-school workflows.

The most direct clinical-placement software vendors appear likely to be private or embedded inside broader healthcare education/workforce SaaS; next pass should search private competitors to map whether any public consolidator owns comparable assets.
HSTM should be promoted for deeper Layer 2 verification as the most direct public-market candidate tied to clinical placement software and healthcare workforce compliance infrastructure.
UTI is a plausible underfollowed capacity beneficiary because Concorde adds healthcare campus/lab/clinical-experience exposure to a company still often perceived as technical/automotive training.
APEI is a speculative-shadow candidate: nursing education assets are relevant, but clinical placement capacity and segment-level economics require verification before upgrading.
The node appears investable through three public-market paths: clinical placement/compliance software, physical healthcare career colleges, and employer/hospital partnership networks.

Many pure simulation-equipment vendors and clinical-placement networks are private; CAE exited healthcare simulation in 2024, so public exposure may be indirect or embedded inside education/workforce software names.
HSTM should be promoted for deeper Layer 2 review as the most direct underfollowed clinical-placement software and healthcare compliance-documentation asset found in this pass.
UTI is a relevant hands-on capacity operator because Concorde adds healthcare campus and clinical-placement exposure while legacy UTI adds trade-school lab and employer-partner exposure.

Clinical placement and simulation capacity are not pure online-learning exposures; the bottleneck appears to be offline throughput, compliance documentation, employer/health-system partnerships, and accredited lab capacity.

The most direct clinical-placement software assets are mostly private or embedded inside broader public companies; later layers should verify whether HSTM's acquired clinical-rotation products are financially material.

HSTM should be retained for Layer 2 as the cleanest direct clinical-placement workflow candidate; evidence priority is product-level revenue or usage growth for myClinicalExchange, TCPS, and The Clinical Hub.

UTI is a plausible underfollowed physical-capacity beneficiary through Concorde healthcare programs and UTI/MIAT skilled-trades campuses; verify whether campus capacity, employer agreements, and externship/clinical placement are actual constraints.

LINC is a more speculative small-cap hands-on training candidate; include only if later evidence shows healthcare-services or skilled-trades capacity additions with measurable employer demand and placement outcomes.

Clinical placement and hands-on training capacity may be a shadow bottleneck because online education demand can scale faster than hospital rotations, lab seats, instructors, accreditation approvals, and employer sites.

Many clinical simulation vendors and clinical-placement tools are private or acquired into larger platforms; future searches should map private competitors such as Laerdal, Gaumard, Exxat, CORE Higher Ed, Sentinel U, and Elevate Healthcare to identify public parents, suppliers, or acquirers.

NNI should be treated as the cleanest public education-finance infrastructure reference name for this node because it combines student-loan servicing, payment technology, and tuition-management exposure, but later layers must separate fee-based servicing from balance-sheet net interest income.

MMS/Aidvantage is a direct federal student-loan servicing contractor and belongs in the reference lane, but materiality is uncertain because student-loan servicing is embedded in broader government-services operations.

FLYW is an underfollowed education affordability/payment-rail candidate because its university receivables, payment-plan, 529, sponsor invoicing, and cross-border tuition workflows sit one step away from student-loan demand.

BFAM/EdAssist is a hidden employer-benefits administration candidate; exposure is likely less pure than FLYW or NNI, but it maps to employer tuition assistance and student-loan repayment benefit administration.

Navient should remain as a watchlist/negative-control name rather than a top Layer 1B candidate for now: it is public and historically tied to education-loan servicing, but federal servicing exit, CFPB settlement/bans, and legacy credit exposure may dominate the infrastructure thesis.

For this node, the best Serenity chokepoint evidence will be contract durability, servicing account volumes, compliance workload, payment-plan adoption, university ERP integration depth, and employer-benefit administration growth—not loan origination volume alone.

NNI should remain a priority underfollowed candidate for the student_finance_servicing node because it combines federal/private education-loan servicing with campus payment-plan and higher-ed payment technology exposure.

FLYW is a second-order education affordability infrastructure candidate: its education vertical, Student Financial Software, payment plans, and cross-border tuition rails map to university finance-office bottlenecks rather than education content.
BFAM/EdAssist is a hidden employer-side affordability rail for workforce education, tuition reimbursement, student-loan repayment, and student-loan retirement-match administration.
Layer 2 should verify market-cap buckets, revenue purity, contract duration, compliance risk, and whether servicing/payment-plan economics are material enough to move each public company.

The node appears to be a regulated/admin chokepoint rather than content supply: scarce capability is compliance-heavy payment/servicing operations, integrations with university/employer systems, and durable contracts under changing student-loan and tuition-benefit rules.

NNI is the most direct underfollowed public candidate for the regulated servicing/payment-infrastructure node, with both Department of Education servicing exposure and education technology/payment platforms.

FLYW is a high-relevance underfollowed payment-rail candidate because education institutions are a large disclosed client category and the company supports tuition payment plans, cross-border payments, and student financial software.
BFAM/EdAssist is a hidden employer-benefits administration candidate for tuition assistance and student-loan repayment, but materiality to consolidated BFAM must be verified.

The strongest chokepoint framing is not education content creation; it is compliant administration across loan servicing, tuition receivables, employer repayment benefits, payment plans, and regulatory/customer data workflows.

Layer 2 should verify federal policy exposure, contract durability, customer concentration, fee-based versus balance-sheet revenue mix, and whether education-affordability products are large enough to move company-level financials.
NNI is the cleanest public candidate for the student_finance_servicing node because it combines federal/private loan servicing scale with education technology and payment administration segments.
FLYW is a second-order education affordability infrastructure candidate via tuition payment rails, payment plans, collections, and international student payment workflows.
BFAM should be tracked as a hidden employer education-benefit and student-loan-repayment administrator through EdAssist, not merely as a child-care services company.
The stronger underfollowed lane appears to be fee-based servicing, payment administration, and employer reimbursement infrastructure rather than balance-sheet-heavy private student lenders.

Later layers must verify federal student-loan policy exposure, Department of Education contract economics, customer concentration, segment materiality, and whether student-loan repayment/tax-benefit rules remain favorable.
FA should be promoted to Layer 2 verification as the cleanest underfollowed public candidate for education/work-history verification and credential screening.
EFX is the public reference anchor for employment/income verification data; use it to map dependencies of smaller background-screening vendors and payroll integrations.
COUR is a mid-cap skills/credential platform candidate, but later layers must prove that credentials are employer-recognized and monetized beyond generic online learning.

Pure-play labor-market analytics leaders such as Lightcast and Chmura appear private based on current evidence, leaving limited US-listed pure-play exposure; later searches should inspect HR/payroll software, staffing, and public-sector workforce analytics vendors for second-order public proxies.
Add FA as a direct underfollowed public candidate for credential, education, work-history, identity, and background verification exposure inside the education-to-employment data node.
Add COUR as a small-cap public candidate where the chokepoint angle is not generic online learning but skills graph, verified credentials, learner records, and employer/university pathway data.
Add PCTY as a second-order payroll/HCM data-pipe candidate feeding employment verification networks; treat as inference until monetization and scale are verified in filings.
Use EFX as the reference leader for employment/income verification infrastructure; not an underfollowed alpha lane but useful for benchmarking scale, regulation, data coverage, and pricing power.

Private/non-listed assets appear important in this node, especially Lightcast for labor-market analytics and National Student Clearinghouse for education records; later layers should map which public companies depend on or compete with these private utilities.

FA is a high-priority underfollowed candidate for the credential-verification node because it directly offers identity, background screening, education/work verification, credential checks, and ongoing monitoring, and absorbed Sterling Check in 2024.

DCBO is a small-cap hypothesis for skills-data and learner-record infrastructure after adding 365Talents skills intelligence and exposing learning/certification context to AI tools; needs proof of monetization and adoption.

COUR is a small-cap direct-but-debated candidate because its Skills Graph, Career Graph, Skills Verification, and micro-credential platform connect learners, skills, credentials, institutions, employers, and governments.
EFX/The Work Number should be treated as a reference anchor and potential dependency layer for employment and income verification, not as an underfollowed education pure play.

Pearson PLC / Pearson VUE may be a relevant US-listed ADR certification-gate candidate, but it was excluded due to the four-candidate limit; next pass should test professional certification exposure versus market-cap purity.

Lightcast appears highly relevant to labor-market analytics and education-workforce alignment, but current evidence indicates it is private/KKR-backed, so it is not a direct US-listed candidate; use it as a private benchmark when evaluating public substitutes.
PSO/Pearson should remain the reference leader for digital credentialing because Credly provides direct verified-skills and credential-network exposure.

FA/First Advantage is the best underfollowed mid-cap candidate found in this pass: education exposure is hidden inside background screening, credential verification, identity, ATS/HCM integrations, and hiring compliance workflows.
COUR/Coursera should be tracked not only as online learning but also as a proprietary skills-signal and microcredential data asset; verify monetization beyond enrollment.

SKIL/Skillsoft is a below-$300M speculative exception with direct skills-management language; survival depends on balance sheet, customer adoption, and whether Percipio skills data creates defensible recurring revenue.

Equifax was not included due to the four-candidate limit and large-cap status, but its Work Number and Verification of Education products make it an important large-cap adjacent verification anchor for later comparison.

The chokepoint may not be course delivery; it may be trusted verification rails and interoperable skills data connecting transcripts, badges, licenses, employment history, ATS/HCM systems, and workforce planning.

Education chain should be mapped as demand drivers plus regulated throughput nodes: healthcare labor demand, clinical placement access, lab capacity, instructor supply, licensure content, assessment integrity, credential verification, student-finance rails, and employer-funded workforce pipelines.

Highest-priority bottleneck is clinical placement and healthcare-network access, because online coursework cannot substitute for regulated clinical hours, supervision, compliance documentation, and hospital affiliation agreements.

Second high-priority bottleneck is physical vocational and healthcare training capacity: campuses, instructors, labs, simulation equipment, manufacturer/employer relationships, and local placement channels.

Student finance, tuition payments, loan servicing, and affordability infrastructure are hidden second-order nodes that can benefit from complexity even when traditional enrollment headlines are mixed.
Assessment integrity and credential verification become more important as online/hybrid learning and AI-enabled cheating increase the need for trusted proof of identity, skill, and education history.

Track hospital affiliation announcements, ABSN site launches, employer-funded training partnerships, campus openings, clinical faculty hiring, accreditation actions, placement-rate disclosures, and gainful-employment policy changes.

Need primary-source validation from latest 10-Ks, 10-Qs, investor decks, accreditation databases, state nursing-board approvals, Department of Education data, and earnings-call transcripts before company-level ranking.
Need to verify whether hidden education-exposed segments are financially material for diversified names such as Graham Holdings, Pearson, Nelnet, Flywire, First Advantage, and HealthStream.
Need market-pricing check in later layers: current valuation, revenue mix, segment growth, short interest, consensus expectations, and whether education chokepoint exposure is already widely priced.
HSTM should be tracked as an underfollowed healthcare-education workflow supplier, especially around clinical-placement coordination, credentialing, and compliance-documentation throughput.

LOPE should be tracked as an underfollowed hybrid healthcare-education infrastructure operator through Orbis/ABSN and partner-university services rather than only as a generic education-services company.

ATGE should remain a reference healthcare-education operator for nursing/allied-health demand and clinical-affiliation capacity, useful as a benchmark for the more obscure suppliers and capacity owners.

NNI should be mapped to regulated student-finance and repayment-administration infrastructure; the key survival test is whether fee-based servicing/payment activity offsets legacy loan runoff and contract volatility.
GHC should be tracked as a hidden education-content and licensure-prep exposure through Kaplan inside a diversified holding company.

UTI should be tracked as a physical vocational and allied-health training capacity owner where labs, instructors, equipment, employer relationships, and placement outcomes are the core bottleneck variables.

FA should be tracked as a second-order credential-verification and background-screening infrastructure candidate, but current evidence is weaker and needs product-level education/work verification attach-rate proof.
FLYW should be tracked as education payment-rails infrastructure, especially cross-border tuition payments and university collections/payment-plan outsourcing.

LINC is an adjacent speculative shadow candidate for skilled-trades physical capacity and hybrid vocational delivery, but it was not part of the cached candidate chunk and needs primary-source validation before promotion.
Need fresh market-cap, analyst-coverage, segment-revenue, and customer-concentration checks for HSTM, LOPE, ATGE, NNI, GHC, UTI, FA, and FLYW before confirming underfollowed status or prioritization.

Need primary-source regulatory checks across Title IV, gainful employment, accreditation, state authorization, professional licensure, Department of Education loan servicing, and outcome-reporting rules.

Need falsification tests by node: weak student starts, low utilization, placement deterioration, clinical-slot shortages, university insourcing, payment take-rate compression, screening-volume cyclicality, regulatory sanctions, and segment disclosure opacity.
COUR is the cleanest candidate in this chunk for the certificate/skills-graph layer; its importance rises if employer acceptance and enterprise retention improve.
EFX and PCTY form an upstream verification-data rail for the education-to-employment stack, while DCBO is the likely workflow/software layer that could store skill and compliance records.
APEI and STRA are more operator-like and should be treated as execution-dependent beneficiaries of workforce demand, not pure infrastructure plays.
Need fresh public filings and segment disclosures to verify revenue mix, customer concentration, and adoption metrics for COUR, DCBO, and PCTY before upgrading the hidden-asset thesis.
Need current market-cap, analyst coverage, and customer reference checks to confirm which of these remain genuinely underfollowed versus merely small-cap or unloved.

FC maps to workforce training and continuing education as a speculative-shadow name; relationship remains a hypothesis until filings show meaningful education-practice revenue, continuing-education credit demand, recurring renewal strength, or institutional education/government contract growth.

SKIL maps to enterprise learning, compliance training, skills data, and learner-record infrastructure; relationship remains a hypothesis due to micro-cap/turnaround risk and unverified evidence that skills-data functionality drives retention or pricing power.

BKYI maps to assessment integrity and education IAM only as a micro-cap speculative exception; survival in the funnel requires direct evidence of education customers, testing workflows, LMS/proctoring partnerships, or secure assessment authentication use cases.

IDN maps to exam-security and credentialing identity verification only as speculation; the current packet has no direct education relationship evidence, so next work must look for testing-vendor, licensing-board, university, admissions, or credentialing-platform relationships.

For all four tickers, market-cap, liquidity, analyst coverage, revenue segment materiality, and current financial condition require fresh verification before upgrading or downgrading underfollowed status.

Need primary-source validation from latest 10-K/10-Q filings, earnings transcripts, investor decks, customer case studies, procurement databases, and partnership announcements; current evidence mainly supports candidate inclusion rather than investment thesis confirmation.
